findings.claim: All 42 practice questions across lessons 1-7 label the Shakespeare tasks "15 marks — Extract Response" (14 of them) and "25 marks — Essay Response" (14 of them), and every band ladder is built on those totals (Top band 13–15 / 21–25 and so on). The remaining 14 are the house "4 marks — Quote Analysis" short questions.
findings.truth: Edexcel Section A is a two-part question worth 20 + 20. Part (a) is 20 marks, AO2 only, on a printed extract of about 30 lines. Part (b) is 20 marks, AO1 15 + AO3 5, on how a theme from the extract is explored elsewhere in the play. There is no 15 + 25 split and no AO4 or SPaG mark on this section. Relabelled to 20 marks each and the band ladder rebuilt as 17–20 / 13–16 / 9–12 / 5–8 / 1–4.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md lines 1102-1113 (two-part question, part a AO2 on a ~30-line extract, part b AO1 and AO3, 80 marks, 1h45, closed book) and the raw-mark table at lines 1312-1350 (Questions 1a-6a: AO2 20; Questions 1b-6b: AO1 15 + AO3 5)

findings.claim: Seven whole-play stems copy another board's formula: "Starting with Act 1, Scene 3, explore how... Write about the extract and the play as a whole" (lessons 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7) and "You should consider both the extract and the play as a whole" (lesson 1). Lesson 7's version says "Starting with the extract" without naming any extract at all.
findings.truth: Edexcel part (b) does not ask students to write about the extract again. It names what the extract shows, then asks how that theme is explored elsewhere in the play. Rewritten to that shape: "In this extract from Act 2, Scene 2, Shakespeare uses blood imagery to present guilt. Explain how guilt is explored elsewhere in the play."
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md line 1108: "Part b) is focused on how a theme from the extract is explored elsewhere in the play"; also line 439

findings.claim: Practice question 5 ("How does Shakespeare use the witches' speech patterns to present them as existing outside the natural order?") is typed as an extract response but names no extract.
findings.truth: Part (a) is always set on a printed extract. The mark scheme for this question analyses the metre, the rhyming couplets and the brevity of Act 1, Scene 1, so the stem now points at that scene.

findings.claim: “Component 1, Section A requires you to show understanding of the relationship between the text and the context in which it was written (AO3).”
findings.truth: The statement itself is correct for Edexcel, but “Component 1” is a banned spec code in lesson text and would fail the whole unit at validation. Replaced with “The Shakespeare question”.

findings.claim: “demonstrates sophisticated understanding of AO3.” (lesson 1) and “Both perspectives are valid for AO3.” (lesson 6)
findings.truth: An AO code immediately followed by a full stop is rejected by the house validator as a spec-code pattern. Reworded to “...understanding of context (AO3).” and “...valid for context (AO3).”
Macbeth says Duncan’s “virtues / Will plead like angels”. The quotation marks enclose a word that is not in the play.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1533 line 884: “Will plead like angels, trumpet-tongued, against” (Act 1, Scene 7)

findings.truth: The line is “Signifying nothing”. The tip tells students to analyse a word Shakespeare did not write.

findings.claim: Flashcard 14 gives Malcolm’s king-becoming graces inside quotation marks as “Justice, verity, temperance, mercy, devotion, patience, courage, fortitude.”
findings.truth: Malcolm names twelve graces: “justice, verity, temperance, stableness, / Bounty, perseverance, mercy, lowliness, / Devotion, patience, courage, fortitude”. Four are dropped with no ellipsis. Not edited: a short flashcard answer that is a comma list is rejected by the validator, so a safe rewrite is not available at flashcard length. The lesson prose around it is correct.

findings.claim: The falcon killed by an owl and the horses eating each other in Act 2, Scene 4 are called “pathetic fallacy”.
findings.truth: Those two events are unnatural portents, not pathetic fallacy; only the darkened sky (“dark night strangles the travelling lamp”) fits the usual definition. The lesson’s own glossary defines pathetic fallacy widely enough to cover them, and the usage is common in GCSE teaching, so this is recorded rather than edited.

summary: The play content is strong: every quotation in all seven lessons is verbatim and correctly attributed to the right speaker and scene, and the context (James I, Daemonologie 1597, the 1604 Witchcraft Act, the Gunpowder Plot, Holinshed, the descent from Banquo) checks out. The unit's fault is board-wide: all 28 Shakespeare practice questions and their band ladders sit on a 15 + 25 split where Edexcel is 20 + 20, and seven part (b) stems use another board's "write about the extract and the play as a whole" formula. One banned spec code in lesson 1 would have failed the whole unit. Lessons 2, 3, 4 and 7 carry no error of their own beyond that unit-wide question format.
